plot_extraction.response_text:
Frances returns home from Liverpool heartsick after learning that Jimmy, the man she has loved for years despite his lukewarm interest, is engaged. While resting on the common with her practical younger sister Anne, she watches Anne capture and then abruptly kill a mole that bites her. The creature’s death shocks Frances but also hardens her, replacing her acute sadness with weary indifference.

The sisters later meet Tom Smedley, a local man who has long been willing to court Frances. Since Jimmy is no longer available, Frances decides she will accept Tom as a second choice. Their flirtatious but tense conversation centers on whether she is capable of killing moles, and Tom’s challenge becomes an implicit test of her willingness to enter his world and accept him.

The next day Frances deliberately hunts down and kills another mole, then brings its body to Tom as proof. Recognizing her gesture as an invitation, Tom asks her to go out with him and says they must tell her mother. Frances agrees without enthusiasm, yet feels a troubling pleasure in surrendering to this new relationship and in letting her former hopes die.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses close third-person narration, moving chiefly through Frances’s unstable emotional perspective while occasionally entering Anne’s and Tom’s consciousness. The narrator combines psychological intimacy with an assured, sometimes aphoristic overview of character: Anne is practical and “unvexed,” Frances whimsical and wounded, and Tom instinctive but emotionally inarticulate. Feelings are rarely explained in purely abstract terms; instead, they are registered through bodily reactions, glances, gestures, changes of attention, and the shifting appearance of the physical world.

The prose is sensuous, richly visual, and strongly rooted in the rural landscape. Colour terms recur with painterly precision—brown, scarlet, blonde, khaki, ruby, blackish—and natural objects are rendered through unusual textures and comparisons. The countryside is not decorative background but an emotional medium. Heat, glare, scorched vegetation, stillness, fruit, stubble, and dry earth reflect Frances’s exhaustion and estrangement. As her emotional condition changes, the landscape changes in value: objects first possess an intense, almost hostile poignancy, then become “trifling” after the mole’s death. Nature is therefore both vividly material and symbolically responsive.

Sentence structure alternates between compact dramatic statements and long, cumulative descriptive passages. Dialogue and moments of violence are handled with short clauses, abrupt turns, and precise physical verbs, while landscape descriptions expand through lists, parallel constructions, semicolons, and layered spatial perspectives. Repetition is used to intensify sensation, especially in the mole episode, where its blindness, frantic movement, small hands, and gaping mouth are described several times from slightly altered angles. This creates a slow, almost unbearable scrutiny before the sudden simplicity of its death.

The diction mixes literary description with colloquial, regionally marked speech. Forms such as “appen,” “s’ll,” “wi’,” “yon,” “nay,” and “moudiwarp” establish a working rural community and expose differences of class, education, and aspiration. Anne’s speech is direct, comic, and practical; Tom’s dialect conveys both social rootedness and vulnerability; Frances’s more standard speech reflects refinement, self-consciousness, and her attraction to gentility. Speech itself becomes part of courtship when Frances asks Tom to “talk nicely,” superficially correcting him while actually inviting intimacy.

Dialogue is highly subtextual. Characters speak about rabbits, engagements, dialect, and moles while negotiating jealousy, sexual attraction, pride, class, and emotional power. Exchanges often proceed through teasing contradiction, evasive questions, and sudden tonal shifts. Frances habitually protects herself with sarcasm, coldness, or flippancy, whereas Anne’s literal-minded interventions provide comic relief and expose what the adults are avoiding. Tom’s courtship is hesitant and oblique, expressed through verbal awkwardness and physical agitation rather than polished declaration.

Characterization depends upon contrast. Anne is younger but behaves maternally; she is vigorous, affectionate, complacent, and capable of swift practical violence. Frances is older yet more fragile, divided between longing, pride, cruelty, and the desire to surrender. Tom is socially less refined than Frances’s idealized Jimmy, but he possesses a physical and emotional force that Jimmy’s distant “half-measures” lack. These oppositions—practicality and sensitivity, refinement and instinct, detachment and desire—generate the story’s tension.

The mole functions as the central symbolic image and structural hinge. Its ecstatic but blind exposure to heat and touch parallels Frances’s emotional vulnerability, while its killing dramatizes the destruction of helpless feeling. Frances’s pity gives way to indifference, and she subsequently repeats the act herself. Bringing Tom the second dead mole becomes a displaced erotic offering and proof that she can accept his harsher, earthbound world. The symbol remains deliberately ambivalent: killing the mole suggests emotional deadening and compromised choice, but also decision, agency, and entry into adult sexuality.

The tone shifts fluidly among rustic comedy, lyrical pastoral description, psychological unease, cruelty, and restrained erotic intensity. Humour arises from Anne’s bluntness, Tom’s dialect, and the sisters’ teasing, but it never cancels the underlying sadness. Violence is presented without melodramatic commentary; its emotional force comes from exact observation and Frances’s changing response. The final courtship scene is similarly unsentimental. Desire appears as something bodily, frightening, coercive, and tender at once.

Structurally, the story moves from fatigue and romantic disappointment through symbolic death to a substitute attachment. The progression is quiet but tightly controlled: Frances hears of Jimmy’s engagement, witnesses Anne kill a mole, tests Tom through the language of killing, then kills another mole and offers it to him. Recurring images and phrases bind these stages together. The ending preserves emotional ambiguity through paradox: Frances answers in a “dead voice,” yet experiences “a thrill of pleasure in this death.” This fusion of loss and gratification typifies the story’s style, which treats love not as uncomplicated fulfilment but as a troubling mixture of surrender, displacement, pride, violence, and renewed vitality.

generation.response_text:
Frances came home from Liverpool in the afternoon, when the August heat lay flattened over the fields and every hedge seemed to have gathered dust into its leaves. She walked from the station because there was no trap waiting. The road, white between the banks, dazzled her; tar softened beneath her shoes, and the iron hoops of the gates burned scarlet where the sun struck them.

She carried a little brown case. It was not heavy, but before she reached the common it had dragged her shoulder down, and her gloved hand felt swollen round the handle.

Anne had come to meet her by the footpath. She appeared above the bracken suddenly, bare-headed, her blonde hair roughened by the wind, though there was scarcely any wind below. She wore an old khaki skirt and carried a basket with two rabbits in it, their feet stiffly projecting under a cloth.

“You’re late,” she said.

“I came by the train I said.”

“Ay, but it was late.”

“Then I am not late.”

Anne looked at her sister’s pale, heated face, and took the case without asking. She was five years younger, broader in the shoulder, and had the comfortable, unquestioning strength of one who had never expected life to arrange itself delicately for her.

“Did you see him?” she asked.

Frances pulled off one glove finger by finger.

“Yes.”

“And?”

“He is engaged.”

Anne said nothing. She shifted the case to her other hand and turned towards home. The two rabbits knocked softly against the basket as she moved.

Frances waited for sympathy, but when none came she laughed.

“You might say something.”

“What’s there to say?”

“That you are sorry, perhaps.”

“I am sorry if you are.”

“That is generous.”

They walked a little way. The common dipped before them, brown and purple, with hollows of burnt grass and low bushes whose blackish berries had shrivelled before ripening. Beyond it, the stubble rose towards the village in bands of yellow glare. A few cattle stood near the pond, their legs dark in the shallow water, their heads bowed as if in penitence.

“Is she pretty?” Anne asked.

“I don’t know.”

“You saw her?”

“I saw a photograph. She has pearls and a long neck.”

“Like a goose?”

“Not in the least like a goose.”

Anne considered this.

“What did he say?”

“He said he hoped I should like her.”

“And will you?”

“I shall adore her. I shall embroider her initials on everything I possess.”

Anne gave a short laugh. Frances disliked her for laughing and was grateful to her at the same instant.

They reached a thorn tree which cast a small, defective shade. The earth beneath was dry and powdered with the dung of sheep. Frances sat down abruptly, leaning her back against the trunk. She took off her hat and laid it in her lap. The hat had looked pretty in Liverpool; here its grey ribbon appeared affected and limp.

“I can’t go farther yet.”

“You’ll get ants on you.”

“I don’t care.”

Anne put down the case and basket. She sat with her knees raised, her brown forearms resting upon them, and looked across the common. Frances closed her eyes.

At once Liverpool returned: the hotel lounge with its ruby carpet, the palms in brass pots, Jimmy bending over her hand with a tender concern that had never ripened into tenderness. He had been kind. That was the intolerable thing. He had ordered tea and moved the little silver strainer towards her; he had spoken of Evelyn’s music, Evelyn’s people, Evelyn’s charming ignorance of the north. All the while he had watched Frances with his clear, mild eyes, asking her to help him make the occasion graceful.

She had helped. She had even smiled.

Now a grasshopper sprang against her skirt, and she shuddered.

“I suppose you always knew,” she said.

“Knew what?”

“That he would marry someone else.”

“I reckoned he might.”

“Because no one could marry me?”

“Nay. Because he never seemed set on it.”

Frances opened her eyes. The sky above the common was nearly white, emptied by heat. A hawk hung in it, no larger than a dark nail.

“He cared for me.”

“Appen.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means appen he did.”

“You are hateful.”

Anne plucked a stalk of grass and bit the pale end.

“I never liked him,” she said.

“Of course not. He spoke properly and kept his nails clean.”

“So does parson.”

Frances turned away. The objects about her had acquired a cruel distinctness: the split casing of a chestnut under her hand; a strand of sheep’s wool caught on a thorn; the yellow dust in the seams of Anne’s boots. Each thing persisted, complete and needless, while the life Frances had secretly composed for herself fell to pieces without making a sound.

For years she had loved Jimmy in futures. Next winter he would understand. At Christmas he would come. When his prospects improved, when his mother ceased objecting, when Frances had a better dress, when they were both older and less afraid—then his half-smiles and half-confidences would join into certainty. She had lived among these postponed arrivals until they seemed more substantial than any day she actually inhabited.

Now he was engaged to a woman with pearls.

Anne sat up.

“What’s that?”

There was a movement in the thin grass, not the glide of a snake nor the quick neat flight of a mouse, but a blunt, laborious disturbance of the soil. A small mound lifted, cracked, and subsided. Then, as if pushed upward by the heat itself, a mole broke through.

It came into the light foolishly. Its black fur had a bluish bloom, soft as soot beneath glass. Its pointed nose worked with desperate delicacy; the pale hands, spread sideways, paddled at the hard surface. It moved in a crooked rush, stopped, opened its pink mouth, and rushed again.

“Oh!” Frances said. “Poor thing.”

Anne was already on her knees.

“Don’t touch it.”

“It’ll spoil the pasture.”

“What can that one little creature spoil?”

“More than you’d think.”

Anne dropped her hat over it. The felt twitched and travelled an inch. Frances leaned forward, suddenly intent. Beneath the crown there was a frantic scratching, minute yet violent, like rain trapped in a box.

“Let it go,” she said.

“I want to see it.”

Anne slipped her hand under the brim. A moment later she cried out and flung the hat aside.

The mole lay exposed, its mouth wide, its blind head lifted. One of Anne’s fingers showed a bright bead of blood.

“It bit me!”

“Of course it bit you. You were crushing it.”

“I weren’t crushing it.”

The mole turned upon itself. Its hands, absurdly broad and human, seized nothing; its body shone black in the sun. It seemed naked despite its fur, all appetite and terror, thrust into a world for which it had no eyes.

Anne caught up the rabbit basket.

“No,” Frances said.

Anne brought the wooden rim down.

There was a soft blow. The creature contracted.

Anne struck again, more accurately. The small mouth remained open, but the body no longer answered it. One forefoot was doubled under; the other rested palm-upward upon the dust.

For several seconds neither sister moved.

“You beast,” Frances whispered.

“It bit me.”

“You could have let it go.”

“And have it digging?”

“It was alive.”

“So’s everything till it’s dead.”

Anne sucked her finger. She was disturbed less by the killing than by Frances’s gaze, which made her feel large and clumsy. Yet beneath this discomfort she remained sure. A mole in a pasture was damage; a bite was pain; a blow ended both. Things were vexatious chiefly when people refused to finish them.

Frances stared at the little black body. She expected pity to rise in her again, sharp and luxurious. Instead something in her went level.

The chestnut casing, the wool on the thorn, the shrivelled berries—suddenly they were merely things. The hawk was gone. The sun still pressed on her forehead, but it no longer accused her. Even Jimmy’s engagement seemed to have moved away from the centre of existence. A mole had struggled, bitten, and been killed. There was no appeal beyond the fact.

“Give us your hand,” Anne said.

Frances bound the bitten finger with her handkerchief.

“You’ve spoiled it with blood.”

“It’ll wash.”

“It was a good handkerchief.”

“Then you shouldn’t have offered.”

Frances laughed, wearily and without resentment. They left the mole beside the thorn tree, a small black knot upon the immense brown common, and went home.

Near the lane they met Tom Smedley coming through a gate. He had a fork over his shoulder and his shirt-sleeves rolled high. The sun had darkened his face and arms, but under the brim of his hat his eyes looked unexpectedly light. He was not handsome in the manner Frances admired. His nose was too broad, his mouth uncertain when he smiled, and his clothes always seemed to contain traces of whatever work he had last done—straw, flour, horsehair, the green smell of bruised stems.

He stopped when he saw her.

“Well, Fran. Back from Liverpool?”

“So it appears.”

“Had a good time?”

“Magnificent.”

Anne said, “Jimmy’s got engaged.”

Tom’s hand tightened on the fork handle. He looked at Frances, then at the road.

“Has he, now?”

“To a girl with a long neck,” Anne continued.

“Anne!”

“Well, she has.”

Tom attempted a laugh.

“Then he’s suited hisself, I reckon.”

“Perfectly,” Frances said. “We must all be glad when people suit themselves.”

He heard the brittleness in her voice without knowing what to do with it. He had wanted Frances for so long that his desire had lost the shape of hope and become a condition, like weather in the bones. Jimmy belonged to that upper, polished region from which letters came and motorcars descended. Tom had resented him without daring to despise him. Now that the man was removed, Tom felt not triumph but a rough alarm. The empty place beside Frances seemed more dangerous than when occupied.

“What’s happened to your finger, Annie?” he asked.

“A moudiwarp bit me.”

“A mole,” Frances said.

“Ay, a moudiwarp. Did you finish him?”

“I killed it with basket.”

Tom grinned. “That’s my lass.”

Frances looked at him.

“Is it admirable to kill moles?”

“If they’re in pasture.”

“Suppose they are on the common?”

“They don’t know boundaries.”

“Like men.”

Tom shifted the fork. Anne looked from one to the other, interested.

“Could you kill one?” he asked Frances.

She smiled. “Why should I?”

“Thought you were too tender.”

“Did you?”

“Ay.”

“Speak nicely, Tom.”

He flushed beneath the brown of his face.

“I said, I thought you were too tender.”

“That is not what I meant.”

“What did you mean, then?”

“You know perfectly well.”

“Nay, I don’t.”

“She means don’t say ‘ay’,” Anne explained.

Frances gave her a look, but Tom laughed. His laughter changed him; it came from his chest and made him for an instant easy and young.

“All right,” he said carefully. “Yes, Miss Frances. I believe you are too tender-hearted to kill a mole.”

“You believe nothing of the kind. You think I am useless.”

“I never said useless.”

“You think I can do nothing but wear gloves and go to Liverpool.”

“I’ve seen you milk.”

“Once.”

“And you let bucket over.”

“The cow kicked it.”

“The cow knew.”

Anne burst out laughing. Frances felt a small, hot pleasure at Tom’s attention. It was not the pleasure she had known with Jimmy, made of waiting, interpretation, and inward music. This was closer and more humiliating. Tom’s eyes rested on her mouth, then moved away. His body was conscious of hers, and that consciousness passed between them like the smell of warm iron.

She said, “I could kill your mole.”

“Mine?”

“Any mole you choose.”

He lowered the fork from his shoulder.

“I’d not choose one for you.”

“Because you are afraid I might do it.”

“Because I don’t want you crying over it after.”

“I should not cry.”

“You near cried over Annie’s.”

“That was before.”

Before what, neither asked.

Tom looked at her, puzzled and stirred. The hard little challenge in her voice was not permission, yet he took strength from it. He had never known how to approach her softness; perhaps hardness offered a road.

“Bring me one, then,” he said.

“Dead?”

“It won’t stay in your pocket alive.”

“I don’t put presents in my pocket.”

“Give it me at our gate.”

“And what will you give me?”

The question silenced them. Anne bent to investigate a loose strap on the rabbit basket, though nothing was wrong with it.

Tom’s face became grave. “Appen I’ll think of summat.”

“Perhaps,” Frances said, “you had better begin.”

She took her case from Anne and walked on. She did not turn, but she could feel Tom watching her until the lane bent.

That evening her mother spoke of Jimmy over the cold mutton. She called his conduct unfortunate, though nobody could say he had promised anything. Frances agreed. She passed the mustard, discussed the price of damsons, and went upstairs before dusk.

Her room looked west over the orchard. Fruit hung among the leaves, plums with a dim violet bloom, apples green on one side and flushed on the other. Wasps entered through the open window and struck repeatedly against the pane, unable to understand the invisible refusal.

Frances undressed slowly. In the mirror her shoulders appeared thin and white above her shift. Jimmy had once touched one shoulder while helping with her coat. She had preserved the touch for three years, taking it out secretly and warming herself by it.

Now she tried to summon it and felt almost nothing.

Instead she saw Tom’s forearms, brown and scratched, and the pause after she had asked what he would give her. Shame moved through her, followed by a heavier sensation which was not shame. She lay down, but sleep would not come. Under the orchard, beneath roots and fallen fruit, small blind creatures travelled in darkness, perfectly occupied.

The next morning she took Anne’s old boots and went out alone.

Dew lay in the shade, though the open fields were already hot. She crossed the common to the place where the first mole had died. Its body was gone. Only a flattened mark remained in the dust, and beside it a few blue-black hairs clung to a stone.

For half an hour she saw nothing. Then near the lower meadow she found fresh ridges running through the grass. She stood over them with a spade taken from the tool shed. The absurdity of her position made her smile. She, who had gone to concerts with Jimmy and corrected Tom’s speech, waited beside churned earth to murder an animal for courtship.

The ground trembled.

She drove in the spade too soon. Soil broke apart, showing a narrow, polished tunnel. Nothing moved. She waited again, her palms damp on the handle.

Far off, a cart creaked along the road. Larks rose invisibly, pouring sound into the white sky. The meadow smelled of dry clover and animal warmth. Frances’s grief seemed no longer a wound but an exhaustion settled throughout her limbs.

Another mound lifted near her boot.

She struck.

The blade entered earth with a thick sound. A black body rolled from the broken tunnel, not cut but stunned. It began at once to labour away, its nose jerking, its hands tearing at the grass. The light appeared to torture it. Its mouth opened upon a tiny scarlet interior.

Frances raised the spade.

For a moment she could not bring it down. The creature’s blindness was horrible because it did not know her; it struggled against heat, air, roots, the whole bright weight of the upper world, but not against Frances. She might have been fate, or weather, or nothing.

“Go on,” she said.

Whether to the mole or herself, she did not know.

It found the lip of its tunnel. One pale hand disappeared into safety.

Frances struck with the flat of the spade.

The body leaped once. She struck again.

Then it was quiet.

She stood breathing through her mouth. There was no thunder, no accusation. A butterfly passed over the grass, yellow as a falling petal. The cart continued along the road. Her own hands looked ordinary.

She wrapped the mole in a dock leaf and carried it to Tom.

He was in the yard mending a hurdle. When he saw her come through the gate, his hammer stopped in mid-blow. She wore no hat; loose strands of hair stuck darkly to her temples. Earth marked the front of her dress, and she carried the green parcel in both hands.

“I have brought your present,” she said.

Tom set down the hammer.

She unfolded the leaf on the stone wall. The mole lay there, compact and black, its snout bloodied with soil.

“You did that?”

“Yes.”

“Yourself?”

“No, I persuaded it to die from admiration.”

He did not smile. He looked from the mole to her face. Something in the offering troubled him: its ugliness, its intimacy, the deliberateness of her coming. He understood, without being able to put understanding into words, that she had crossed some distance for him, though perhaps not towards him alone.

“Why did you do it, Fran?”

“You told me to.”

“I were teasing.”

“You should be careful.”

“Ay.”

“Talk nicely.”

“Yes,” he said. “I was teasing.”

She folded the dock leaf over the body again.

“Do you want it?”

“Nay.”

“Then I have wasted my morning.”

“Don’t.”

“Don’t what?”

“Don’t make nowt of it.”

“Nothing,” she corrected, but softly.

He came closer. The yard was still. Behind the stable door a horse shifted and breathed; flies moved upon the warm bricks. Frances could smell sawdust on Tom’s clothes and the bitter green sap of the leaf between her fingers.

“Will you come out wi’ me Sunday?” he asked.

She looked beyond him towards the fields. Stubble glittered on the hill; the hedges were dark seams, and above them the sky stood pale and vacant. Somewhere beyond those fields were the railway and Liverpool and Jimmy arranging his gracious future. The thought reached her faintly, like a bell heard under water.

“Where?”

“Anywhere you like.”

“You will hate that.”

“Then anywhere I like.”

“I may hate that.”

“We’ll both be suited.”

She laughed once. Tom did not. His face had grown strained, and she saw how much he feared her answer. The discovery gave her power, but the power was joyless. She could hurt him. She could also cease resisting.

“You know why you are asking me now,” she said.

“I’ve asked before.”

“Not like this.”

“No.”

“Because Jimmy is engaged.”

“Because you’re here.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It’s all I’ve got.”

He put his hand on the wall near hers. He did not touch her, yet she felt enclosed by his nearness. Unlike Jimmy, he had no elegant escape prepared, no words that would preserve them both from embarrassment. He stood before her with his desire like a farm tool held awkwardly in bare hands—heavy, useful, dangerous.

“We’d have to tell your mother,” he said.

“So soon?”

“She’ll hear.”

“From Anne, certainly.”

“And I want it proper.”

Frances looked down at the dock leaf. A dark moisture had begun to stain it from within. She thought of the mole under the earth, blind but whole; then in the light, frantic; then still. She thought of all the hopes she had fed in secrecy, and how eagerly they had burrowed towards a future that did not exist.

“Yes,” she said.

Tom’s hand closed over hers.

She did not lift her eyes. His palm was rough and hot; the pressure frightened her by its certainty. She had imagined surrender as a radiant thing, the final answer to long refinement of feeling. This was not radiant. It was earth, heat, blood under a leaf, a man who said “nowt” and wanted her enough to be clumsy.

“We’ll tell her tonight,” he said.

“Yes.”

Her voice sounded extinguished, as though another woman had answered from deep inside her.

Yet when his thumb moved once across her knuckles, a slow pleasure went through her—dark, involuntary, almost cruel. She let the wrapped mole slip from her other hand to the dust. Neither of them stooped to retrieve it.

# The Museum of Forgotten Weather

On the morning the rain was scheduled to return, Mara Vale woke to the sound of hammers on the roof.

For one hopeful second, she mistook the tapping for drops.

Then a workman shouted, “Pass me the copper nails,” and the illusion vanished.

Mara lay still beneath her thin summer blanket. The bedroom window stood open, as it had every night for eleven years, but no breeze entered. Beyond the glass, the city shimmered under a white sky. Roofs sagged in the heat. The riverbed was a pale scar between rows of buildings. Even the pigeons had stopped flying by noon.

Today, according to the Ministry of Atmospheric Recovery, the drought would end at four o’clock.

Mara did not believe them.

She dressed in her gray uniform, pinned back her hair, and walked downstairs to the Museum of Forgotten Weather.

The museum occupied the lower floors of her house, though the house had not always been a museum. Once, before Mara was born, it had been a hotel for travelers arriving by riverboat. The lobby still held a brass reception bell and a wall of small wooden boxes where guests had once left their keys. Now each box contained a different kind of memory.

Box seven held the smell of wet pavement.

Box twelve held the silver stillness before snow.

Box twenty-three held the pressure in the ears that came before a thunderstorm.

The memories were sealed in glass vials, wax envelopes, music boxes, and jars with rusted lids. People came from distant districts to see them. Children who had never felt rain pressed their noses to display cases while guides explained umbrellas, puddles, and mud.

On the first floor stood the Hall of Winds. On the second, the Gallery of Clouds. The basement contained the dangerous collections: lightning, hail, fog dense enough to become lost in, and one small tornado preserved inside a green bottle.

Mara was the museum’s curator, caretaker, ticket seller, and only permanent employee.

At eight, she unlocked the front doors.

A crowd was already waiting in the street.

“Is it true?” a woman called.

“Will you close the museum when the rain comes back?” asked someone else.

A boy near the front held up a folded paper boat. “Can I sail this today?”

Mara raised both hands.

“The museum opens at nine,” she said. “The rain, if it arrives, is expected at four. Until then, all exhibits remain available except the storm cellar.”

The crowd murmured at her careful choice of words.

“If it arrives?” said a reporter in a blue hat. “The Ministry guarantees precipitation.”

“The Ministry has guaranteed precipitation six times.”

“But the new machines—”

“Open at nine,” Mara repeated, and shut the doors.

She leaned against them after the crowd’s voices faded.

From the reception desk, a tiny bell rang.

Mara looked up.

The bell had not been touched. It was the old hotel bell, tarnished and cracked, and it rang only when someone brought weather to the museum.

A second chime trembled through the lobby.

Someone was already inside.

Mara took the iron key from her pocket and moved quietly past the Hall of Winds. The exhibits whispered around her. A bottled sea breeze stirred blue ribbons behind glass. A winter gale shook the door of its cabinet. Somewhere overhead, the ceiling creaked beneath the workmen’s boots.

At the end of the corridor stood a girl in a red coat.

She was perhaps nine years old. The coat was far too heavy for the heat, and its hem was dark with moisture.

Mara stopped.

“Where did you come from?”

The girl pointed toward the front doors.

“They were locked.”

“I know.”

“Then how did you enter?”

“I knocked.”

Mara glanced at the corridor windows. Every latch was fastened. There was no sign of a broken pane, no open door, no muddy footprint—although the girl’s black shoes were wet.

“What is your name?” Mara asked.

“June.”

“Do your parents know where you are?”

June shrugged.

Water fell from the cuff of her coat and struck the floor.

Mara stared at the drop. It rested on the tile, round and bright as a glass bead.

“Is that rainwater?”

“No,” June said. “It’s mine.”

From inside the red coat, she produced a jam jar. The jar was filled with a low, dark cloud.

It turned slowly behind the glass.

Mara forgot the heat. She forgot the crowd outside and the men repairing the roof. She forgot, for an instant, how to breathe.

“Where did you get that?”

“I found it.”

“Where?”

“In my room.”

June held out the jar. Thunder, very small and very far away, murmured inside it.

The reception bell rang a third time.

Mara did not take the jar.

“Put it on the desk,” she said.

June obeyed.

Mara circled it carefully. She had spent her life around preserved weather and knew the signs of a false specimen. Steam could be trapped in a bottle. Smoke could be colored. A hidden metal plate could imitate lightning. But this cloud had depth. It folded into itself, gray over violet, alive with invisible currents. Condensation jeweled the inside of the glass.

“What do you want for it?” Mara asked.

“Nothing.”

“Everyone wants something.”

“I want you to let it out.”

Mara looked at her.

“Absolutely not.”

“It doesn’t like the jar.”

“Most weather doesn’t like being contained.”

“Then why do you keep so much of it here?”

The question was simple, almost innocent, but Mara felt it like an accusation.

“Because there isn’t any left outside.”

June lifted her eyes toward the ceiling. “There will be.”

“So the Ministry says.”

“The Ministry is wrong.”

Mara folded her arms. “They say rain will begin at four.”

“It will. But it won’t stop.”

A hammer struck the roof. Thunder answered from the jar.

June continued, “It will rain through the night. By morning, the river will return. By tomorrow evening, the lower streets will be underwater. The Ministry machines will break, but the rain won’t.”

Mara looked toward the window. The sky was blank, bright, and merciless.

“How could you know that?”

“I remember.”

“You’re nine.”

“I remember anyway.”

The girl’s face held no mischief. That troubled Mara more than any smile would have.

Mara picked up the jar. The glass was cold enough to hurt.

“Come with me.”

She led June upstairs, through the Gallery of Clouds. Here, old skies hung in gilded frames: feathery cirrus from the western farms, bruised thunderheads from the coast, a single sunset cloud preserved on the last evening before the drought began. In the center of the gallery stood a long table covered with maps.

Mara set the jar beside a barometer.

The needle spun wildly.

June wandered to a painting of rain over a green field.

“I’ve seen this place,” she said.

“That field is gone. It’s part of the eastern dust flats now.”

“It was yellow before the rain.”

“Wheat.”

“There was a tree.”

Mara glanced at the painting. A willow leaned over the field’s edge.

“Yes.”

“You were sitting under it.”

The room seemed to contract.

Mara placed both hands on the table. “Who told you that?”

June turned. “You did.”

“I’ve never met you.”

“Not yet.”

Mara’s first instinct was to call the Ministry. Her second was to hide the girl. Years of caring for dangerous things had taught her to trust the second instinct, especially when the first involved officials.

She examined June more closely.

The red coat was old-fashioned but well made. One brass button was missing. A faint scar crossed the girl’s left eyebrow. Around her wrist, she wore a blue thread tied in three knots.

Mara knew that thread.

She wore an identical one beneath her sleeve.

Her mother had tied it there when Mara was a child, telling her the knots stood for what had been, what was, and what might yet be. Mara had never removed it. The thread should have decayed years ago, but it remained stubbornly whole.

“Show me your wrist,” Mara said.

June held out her arm.

Mara touched the three knots. They were damp.

“Who tied this?”

“You did.”

A knock sounded downstairs, loud enough to echo through the museum.

“Mara Vale!” called a man’s voice. “Ministry inspection!”

June reached for the jar.

Mara caught her hand. “Leave it.”

“They’ll take it.”

“They take everything,” Mara said. “That doesn’t mean they find everything.”

She opened a cabinet labeled ALTOCUMULUS, removed a tray of harmless white cloud fragments, and placed the jar behind them.

The knocking below became pounding.

Mara led June to the Hall of Winds and unlocked the exhibit known as the North Room. A cold draft slipped through the door, smelling of pine and distant ice.

“Stay here,” Mara said. “Don’t touch anything.”

“Especially the blue fan?”

Mara narrowed her eyes. “Especially the blue fan.”

“I remember.”

Before Mara could question her further, the pounding resumed.

She hurried downstairs and opened the front door.

Minister Halden stood outside with four officers. He was tall, silver-haired, and perfectly dry despite the sweat shining on every other face in the street. Behind him, the waiting crowd had grown. Vendors sold paper umbrellas. Children wore rubber boots inherited from grandparents.

“Curator Vale,” Halden said. “May we speak privately?”

“You brought an audience.”

“I brought witnesses to a historic day.”

“You brought armed officers.”

“History is unpredictable.”

Mara let them enter.

Halden removed his gloves and looked around the lobby. He had visited the museum often during Mara’s childhood, when he was still an engineer and her mother was curator. He had taught Mara how to read a barometer. Later, as Minister, he had ordered half the museum’s collection seized for research.

None of it had produced rain.

“We detected an atmospheric disturbance here at eight-oh-three,” he said.

“This is a weather museum.”

“An active disturbance.”

“The basement leaks.”

“It hasn’t rained in eleven years.”

“Then perhaps it leaks dust.”

Halden’s smile was weary. “Your mother used to make the same kind of joke.”

“My mother liked you.”

“Once.”

Before you took her final storm, Mara thought.

The museum had possessed a complete thunderstorm then, stored across seven copper vessels. Halden’s engineers had carried them away. Something went wrong during the experiment. The vessels ruptured, the laboratory burned, and Mara’s mother disappeared inside a room filled with unnatural fog.

No body was found.

Halden approached the reception desk. A circle of moisture marked the wood where June’s jar had stood.

He touched it with one finger.

The officers saw his expression and reached for their weapons.

“At eight-oh-three,” Halden said softly, “every sensor in the city pointed here.”

“And what did they detect?”

“A storm forming backward.”

Mara said nothing.

“Ordinary storms gather energy and then release it. This signal began with the release. The cause followed after, as if the storm were moving against time.”

Outside, the crowd began counting down the hours until four, though there were still seven to go.

Halden looked toward the staircase.

“What did you receive?”

“Nothing.”

The old reception bell rang.

Mara closed her eyes.

Halden’s gaze shifted to the bell. “The same bell rang when your mother brought us the final storm.”

“It rings when the metal expands.”

“In this heat, it should ring constantly.”

A door slammed upstairs.

One officer drew his pistol.

Mara stepped between him and the staircase. “No weapons near the exhibits.”

A cold gust swept through the lobby.

Visitors outside cheered, believing it was the first sign of changing weather.

Then June appeared at the top of the stairs, her red coat flapping in the wind.

She held the blue fan.

Behind her, winter poured from the North Room.

Frost flowered over the railing. Snow swirled through the gallery. The officers backed away as ice spread across the floor, cracking tiles and whitening the reception desk.

“I told you not to touch that,” Mara said.

“You were going to tell me,” June replied.

Halden stared at the girl.

For the first time, his composure broke.

“Elena?”

The name passed through Mara like lightning.

Elena had been her mother’s name.

June descended one step at a time. “Not exactly.”

Halden gripped the railing. “Where did you come from?”

“After.”

“After what?”

“The rain.”

The winter wind died as abruptly as it had begun. Snow settled over the lobby. Outside, people pressed against the windows, astonished.

June handed Mara the fan.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “This is how it happened before.”

Mara felt cold for reasons unrelated to the exhibit.

“Before?”

June nodded. “He came. I opened the North Room. Then you hid the jar, but he found it.”

Everyone looked toward the stairs.

Halden moved first.

Mara swung the blue fan. A blast of northern wind struck him and the officers, driving them backward into the wall. She seized June’s hand and ran upstairs.

They reached the Gallery of Clouds. Mara locked the door, dragged the map table against it, and retrieved the jar from the cabinet.

The cloud inside had doubled in size.

“How do we stop the flood?” Mara asked.

June shook her head. “I don’t know.”

“You said you remembered.”

“I remember the water. I remember you putting me in a boat. I remember the museum breaking apart.”

Below, Halden shouted orders.

Mara held up the jar. “Does this cause the rain?”

“It begins it.”

“Then we keep it sealed.”

“You did. It broke at four anyway.”

“What if we destroy it now?”

“You tried that too.”

Mara studied the girl’s face. “How many times have you done this?”

“Only once.”

“That doesn’t make sense.”

“It hasn’t happened yet for you.”

Something struck the gallery door.

The table jumped.

June spoke quickly. “Tomorrow night, the city is underwater. You take me to the museum roof. You tie your blue thread around my wrist and tell me the three knots are what was, what is, and what might yet be. Then lightning hits the tornado bottle.”

Mara glanced instinctively toward the basement.

“The tornado escapes,” June continued. “It carries me into the storm. I fall through the cloud and land in my room yesterday morning.”

“Your room where?”

“Here.”

“This is my house.”

“It becomes mine.”

The door shook again. Wood splintered near the lock.

Mara looked at the cloud paintings, the cabinets, the labels written in her mother’s careful hand. She had spent eleven years preserving the past so perfectly that the museum had become a tomb for the future.

“What happened to me?” she asked.

June lowered her eyes.

That was answer enough.

The door burst inward. Halden stumbled through with an officer behind him.

“Give me the storm,” he said.

“You can’t control it.”

“We don’t need to control it. We need to distribute it.”

“It will flood the city.”

“The city can be evacuated.”

“By four?”

His silence was brief but unmistakable.

“You knew,” Mara said.

“We calculated a significant risk.”

“You promised them an end to the drought.”

“Because hope prevents panic.”

“And what prevents drowning?”

Halden took another step. “Eleven years ago, we stripped the sky of its ability to recover. Every experiment since then has failed. That cloud may be the atmosphere correcting itself.”

“It’s a storm moving backward through time.”

“It’s rain.”

“To you, perhaps those are the same thing.”

The jar cracked.

A thin black line appeared near its base.

Thunder rolled under Mara’s hands.

Beyond the windows, the white sky darkened to gray.

From the street came a roar of celebration.

It was three minutes to four.

Halden lunged.

June snatched the jar first.

“Tell me what to do!” she cried.

Mara’s mind raced through the exhibits. Wind, pressure, cold, electricity—pieces of systems separated, labeled, and placed behind glass. Her mother had always said weather died when divided. A storm was not rain or thunder or wind. It was all of them moving together.

The crack widened.

A drop fell onto the table.

At once, rain struck the windows.

The crowd screamed with joy.

Mara ran to the wall and tore down the painting of the eastern field. Behind it was a brass lever designed to open every emergency lock in the museum.

Halden understood.

“No,” he said. “Those exhibits are irreplaceable.”

“That’s the problem.”

She pulled the lever.

Throughout the building, bolts slammed open.

The museum inhaled.

First came the winds. They rushed from their rooms and cabinets, circling the gallery in warm and cold currents. Then clouds spilled from frames, swelling against the ceiling. Fog climbed from the basement stairs. Hail rattled through the corridors. Captive lightning flickered inside the walls.

The green tornado bottle rose from its shelf below and shattered.

The museum exploded into weather.

Halden and the officer were thrown against the map table. Windows burst outward. Clouds rolled into the city. Wind lifted years of dust from rooftops and carried it away in golden sheets.

Mara took the jar from June.

The cloud inside beat against the glass like a heart.

“What might yet be,” Mara whispered.

She opened the lid.

The cloud streamed upward, joining all the weather the museum had kept apart. For one breathless moment, a storm filled the entire building—wild, balanced, and alive.

Then it rose through the broken roof.

Outside, the rain changed.

The heavy, violent drops softened. The black clouds stretched across the city instead of piling over it. Wind drove them east toward the dust flats, then south along the dead river. Thunder rolled, no longer trapped or backward, but moving naturally into the distance.

The river did not return that night.

It returned slowly over the next three months.

By then, green shoots covered the eastern fields. People patched roofs, cleared drains, and learned that rain was not a performance scheduled by a ministry. It arrived when it arrived. Sometimes it disappointed. Sometimes it stayed too long. Mostly, it ignored speeches.

The Museum of Forgotten Weather did not survive.

Without weather, it was only a damaged old hotel with empty cases and water-stained walls.

Minister Halden resigned. Before leaving the city, he sent Mara a parcel containing the brass reception bell. She installed it above the front desk.

The hotel reopened in spring.

Travelers came first by road, then, eventually, by riverboat. They left wet umbrellas in the lobby and complained about damp sheets. Children jumped in puddles outside until their parents dragged them in.

June remained.

She chose the small bedroom above the Gallery of Clouds, though the gallery was now a dining room. Mara never learned exactly where June had first been born or how many futures had vanished when the storm changed. Some questions, like clouds, lost their shape when held too tightly.

One evening, nearly a year after the scheduled rain, Mara and June walked to the eastern fields.

The wheat was still young and green. At the field’s edge stood a willow, little more than a sapling, its narrow leaves shining after a shower.

They sat beneath it.

June wore the red coat, though the evening was warm. The blue thread remained around her wrist, tied in three knots.

“Do you remember this?” Mara asked.

June considered the field.

“No,” she said at last.

Mara smiled.

Above them, clouds moved freely across the sky.
